claim: A single uniform security policy applied across all AI agent types either over-constrains simple agents or under-constrains autonomous ones, because agent types differ fundamentally in threat model.
stance_target: heavy governance scaffolding is required before high-concurrency agent deployment is safe
scope_conditions: enterprise AI agent deployments, as of April 2026
quoted_support: An organization that deploys a single security policy across all agent types will either over-constrain simple agents, creating friction that drives shadow deployment, or under-constrain autonomous agents, leaving critical exposure unaddressed.

claim: Orchestrator/supervisor agents that spawn and coordinate many sub-agents represent the highest-impact single point of failure in multi-agent architectures, because compromising the orchestrator compromises every agent it coordinates.
stance_target: permission scoping and isolation are required before scaling a Director-agent/many-Worker-agent architecture
quoted_support: Compromising an orchestrator affects all agents it coordinates — it is a force multiplier for the attacker... orchestrators require stronger isolation, more rigorous authentication, and more comprehensive monitoring than the agents they manage.

claim: 44 percent of organizations rely on static API keys as their primary agent authentication method, and 78 percent lack documented policies for agent identity lifecycle management.
stance_target: current identity/permission scoping infrastructure is immature relative to a 100+ Worker Agent concurrency target
quoted_support: The CSA Agentic Identity Survey found that 44 percent of organizations rely on static API keys as their primary agent authentication method... 78 percent lacking documented policies for agent identity lifecycle management.

claim: Autonomous agents operating at non-deterministic, high-frequency scale can cause significant damage before human oversight detects deviation, by analogy to Knight Capital's deterministic trading system losing $440 million in 45 minutes due to inadequate circuit breakers.
stance_target: kill-switches and circuit breakers are necessary before granting high autonomy at scale
scope_conditions: automated/autonomous financial trading systems; analogy extended to AI agents
quoted_support: The lesson of Knight Capital — which lost $440 million in 45 minutes due to an automated system operating without adequate circuit breakers — applies directionally: autonomous systems with access to financial markets can cause significant damage before human oversight detects the deviation.

claim: MCP (Model Context Protocol), the dominant tool-integration standard for agents, has documented critical vulnerabilities including pre-authentication remote code execution, and 38-41% of MCP servers lack authentication entirely.
stance_target: permission scoping and sandboxing of tool access is not yet reliably implemented at scale
scope_conditions: MCP server ecosystem, security assessments conducted in early 2026
quoted_support: authentication is optional in many implementations (38 to 41 percent of MCP servers lack authentication according to security assessments)... Between January and February 2026, security researchers filed over 30 CVEs targeting MCP servers, clients, and infrastructure.

claim: A VirusTotal survey of nearly 18,000 MCP server projects found that over 8 percent showed signs of intentional malice.
stance_target: tool/supply-chain governance is required before scaling agent populations that dynamically acquire tools
quoted_support: A VirusTotal survey of nearly 18,000 MCP server projects found that over 8 percent showed signs of intentional malice.

claim: The MINJA memory injection attack, presented at NeurIPS 2025, achieved over 95 percent injection success rates against agent long-term memory using only query-only interaction, and the MemoryGraft technique (Dec 2025) poisoned 47.9 percent of memories retrieved during subsequent operations.
stance_target: autonomous agents with persistent memory are not reliably safe from adversarial compromise without additional controls
scope_conditions: academic red-team research on agent memory systems, 2025
quoted_support: The MINJA attack (presented at NeurIPS 2025) demonstrated that attackers can inject malicious records into an agent's memory through query-only interaction, achieving over 95 percent injection success rates... The MemoryGraft technique (December 2025) showed that implanting fake 'successful experiences' into agent memory... could poison 47.9 percent of memories retrieved during subsequent operations.

claim: Prompt injection vulnerabilities were found in 73 percent of production AI deployments assessed during 2025 security audits, and the EchoLeak zero-click exploit (CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3) demonstrated agents can be hijacked and made to exfiltrate data with no user action and no privilege escalation required.
stance_target: agents acting with minimal human review carry demonstrated real-world exfiltration/compromise risk even without malicious intent on the operator's part
quoted_support: Prompt injection appeared in 73 percent of production AI deployments assessed during security audits in 2025... the first confirmed zero-click prompt injection exploit in a production enterprise AI system.

claim: CSA recommends concrete governance scaffolding -- a 6-layer Agent Security Architecture (Identity, Policy, Guardrails, Execution/sandboxing, Monitoring, Audit) plus circuit breakers (max tokens, max tool calls, max wall-clock time per task) and out-of-process policy engines -- as necessary before scaling autonomous or orchestrator-type agents.
stance_target: heavy governance scaffolding (permission scoping, kill-switches, escalation triggers) is required before scaling multi-agent concurrency
quoted_support: Cost and execution time circuit breakers (maximum tokens per task, maximum tool calls per execution, maximum wall-clock time) provide an additional safeguard against runaway agents... The out-of-process pattern... is the most secure because a compromised agent process cannot override the policy enforcement.

claim: Delegation chains from orchestrator to sub-agent frequently fail to narrow permissions, with sub-agents commonly inheriting the orchestrator's full permission set, an OWASP-classified privilege escalation risk (ASI03).
stance_target: permission scoping is not yet a solved problem for multi-agent delegation, directly relevant to Director-to-Worker-Agent concurrency
quoted_support: Current implementations frequently fail this requirement — sub-agents inherit the orchestrator's full permission set, creating privilege escalation paths that OWASP classifies as ASI03 (Identity and Privilege Abuse).

claim: An agent that behaves safely in 999 out of 1,000 executions may take a dangerous action in the 1,001st due to non-deterministic sampling, meaning pre-deployment testing alone cannot characterize agent safety and runtime behavioral monitoring is mandatory.
stance_target: agent reliability cannot be certified ex-ante at the volumes implied by 100+ concurrent workers; continuous monitoring is required
scope_conditions: any LLM-based agent with probabilistic sampling
quoted_support: An agent that behaves safely in 999 out of 1,000 executions may take a dangerous action in the 1,001st — not because of a bug, but because the model's probabilistic sampling happened to select a different token sequence.
